segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then after fourteen years I went up again to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus along as well.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I went up in response to a revelation, and I laid before them the good news that I proclaim among the Gentiles—but privately, before those of repute—for fear that I might be running, or had run, in vain.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But not even Titus, who was with me, though he was a Greek, was compelled to be circumcised.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But because of the false brothers secretly brought in, who slipped in to spy on the freedom we have in Christ Jesus, so that they might enslave us—

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: to them we did not yield in submission even for a moment, so that the truth of the good news might remain with you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As for those reputed to be something—whatever they were makes no difference to me; God shows no partiality—those of repute added nothing to me.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: On the contrary, when they saw that I had been entrusted with the good news for the uncircumcised, just as Peter had been for the circumcised,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for the one who was at work in Peter for an apostleship to the circumcised was also at work in me for the Gentiles,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and when they recognized the grace given to me, James and Cephas and John, who were reputed to be pillars, gave me and Barnabas the right hand of partnership, so that we should go to the Gentiles and they to the circumcised.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They asked only that we remember the poor, the very thing I was eager to do.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But when Cephas came to Antioch, I opposed him to his face, because he stood condemned.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For before certain people came from James, he used to eat with the Gentiles; but when they came, he began to draw back and separate himself, fearing those of the circumcision.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the rest of the Jews joined him in this hypocrisy, so that even Barnabas was carried away by their hypocrisy.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But when I saw that they were not walking straight in line with the truth of the good news, I said to Cephas in front of everyone,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “If you, though a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how can you compel the Gentiles to live like Jews?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: We are Jews by birth and not sinners from among the Gentiles,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: yet we know that a person is not justified by works of the law but only through faith in Jesus Christ. So we too believed in Christ Jesus, in order to be justified by faith in Christ and not by works of the law, because by works of the law no flesh will be justified.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if, while seeking to be justified in Christ, we ourselves were also found to be sinners, is Christ then a servant of sin? By no means!

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For if I build up again the very things I tore down, I show myself to be a transgressor.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For through the law I died to the law, so that I might live to God. I have been crucified with Christ,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. The life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself up for me.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I do not set aside the grace of God; for if righteousness comes through the law, then Christ died for nothing.

notes.note: The traditional rendering is “gospel,” which today sounds like a religious term or the title of a book. The Greek was an ordinary word for an announcement of good news, used also of public and imperial proclamations. Many modern translations alternate between “gospel” and “good news.”

notes.phrase: so that they might enslave us—
notes.note: Paul’s sentence breaks off here without a main clause, and the translation leaves it broken as the Greek does. Readers must supply something like “the issue arose” or “pressure was applied.” It is disputed whether the “false brothers” were the reason for the Jerusalem visit or people who intervened during it.
Cephas is the Aramaic form of the nickname given to Simon; Peter is its Greek equivalent, and both mean “rock.” Paul uses both names in this chapter (Peter in verses 7–8) for the same man.

Most translations have “the right hand of fellowship.” The Greek word means having something in common and was used of business partnerships as well as friendship. Here the handshake seals a working agreement about who goes to whom, so “partnership” was chosen; the word also implies mutual recognition.

The phrase is literally “those from circumcision.” It may mean Jewish believers who insisted that Gentile converts be circumcised, which is why many translations say “the circumcision party” or “group.” It may also mean Jews more broadly, whose reaction Peter feared. The translation leaves the phrase open.

Greek manuscripts have no quotation marks, and it is unclear where Paul’s words to Cephas end. Some translations carry the speech through verse 21; others, as here, close it at verse 14 and take verses 15–21 as Paul’s reflection addressed to the Galatians. The argument flows continuously either way.

Greek has one word-family where English has two: “justify” here and “righteousness” in verse 21 share a single root, as do “just” and “righteous.” To be “justified” is to be declared or set in the right. Some scholars prefer “justice” or “vindicate” to keep the link visible in English.

The law in view is the law of Moses. The traditional understanding is that “works of the law” means deeds done in obedience to its commandments generally. Many recent scholars think Paul has especially in mind the practices that marked Jews off from Gentiles—circumcision, food laws, and Sabbath—which are the issues at stake in this chapter. The closing words of the verse echo Psalm 143:2.

The Greek is literally “faith of Jesus Christ,” and “faith of Christ” later in the verse. The traditional and still majority reading is “faith in Christ,” meaning the believer’s trust. A substantial body of scholars reads it as “the faithfulness of Jesus Christ,” meaning his own faithful obedience. The grammar allows both.

notes.phrase: faith in the Son of God
notes.traditional: faith in the Son of God
notes.note: As in verse 16, the Greek is literally “faith of the Son of God.” It can also be read as “the faithfulness of the Son of God,” which would connect naturally with the words that follow about his love and self-giving. The majority reading is followed here.

candidates.reason: Recurs throughout Paul with senses from physical body to humanity to the sinful sphere, and translations vary widely (“flesh,” “sinful nature,” “human being”).
Needs a single decision on capitalization and on whether to supply the article when Paul writes it without one, since “law,” “the law,” and “the Law” read differently.
Used both for the rite and as shorthand for Jews as a group (with ἀκροβυστία for Gentiles); renderings such as “the circumcision,” “the circumcised,” and “Jews” should be fixed.
A central term across the letters where “grace,” “favor,” and “gift” are all defensible and inconsistent choices would obscure Paul’s argument.
The formula μὴ γένοιτο recurs in Romans, 1 Corinthians, Galatians, and Luke and should have one fixed English form.

warnings: Verse 7: πιστεύω is not rendered with a register form (believe / trust) and has no register-exception note.
Verse 20: παραδίδωμι is not rendered with a register form (hand over; hand on; hand down; give up; give over; entrust; risk; be ripe) and has no register-exception note.
